---
title: Navigating The File System
---

First thing that we need to learn when start with command-line is to figure out
how to nagivate the file system. In this chapter, we'll learn about the
following commands:

* `pwd` - print the present working directory
* `cd` - change directory
* `mkdir` - make a directory

We already know `ls` from the previous chapter, and we'll keep using it here to
see where we have ended up.

## Files live in a tree

Every file on your computer sits inside a directory, and every directory sits
inside another directory. It looks like this:

```
/
├── home
│   └── anand
│       ├── notes.txt
│       └── todo.txt
├── usr
│   ├── bin
│   └── share
└── etc
```

At the very top is a single directory called `/`, said "root". Everything else
is somewhere inside it. There is no second tree, and nothing sits outside this
one - every file on the machine has a place in it.

Your own files live in a directory of your own, named after you. Mine is
`/home/anand`. This is called your **home directory**.

## Present Working directory

The `pwd` command prints the present working directory.

```session
$ pwd
/home/anand
```

The present working directory is simply where you are standing right now. Every
command you type runs from there, so it is worth knowing.

When you login, it would typically be your home directory.

## Changing directory

The `cd` command is used to change the present working directory.

The following command changes the current working directory to `/usr`.

```session
$ cd /usr
```

The `cd` command does not produce any output. It moves you, and says nothing
about it. To see that it worked, ask `pwd`:

```session
$ pwd
/usr
```

And now `ls` shows the files in `/usr`, not the ones in your home directory:

```session
$ ls
bin    include  lib32  libexec  local  share
games  lib      lib64  libx32   sbin   src
```

This is the important part: `ls` did not change. *You* changed. `ls` always
lists the directory you are standing in.

You can always come back to your home directory by simply running the `cd`
command without any arguments.

```session
$ cd
```

```session
$ pwd
/home/anand
```

If you try to go somewhere that does not exist, `cd` tells you so:

```session
$ cd nosuchdir
bash: cd: nosuchdir: No such file or directory
```

You have not moved, and nothing is broken. `pwd` will confirm you are still
where you were.

## Absolute and Relative Paths

When we use a path starting with `/`, we are mentioning the full path starting
from the root. `/usr/bin` means: start at the root, go into `usr`, then into
`bin`. This is called an **absolute path**. It means the same thing no matter
where you are standing when you type it.

We could also specify the path relative to the current directory. Let's go to
`/usr` first:

```session
$ cd /usr
```

```session
$ pwd
/usr
```

We know from the `ls` above that `/usr` contains a directory called `bin`. So
from here, we can just say:

```session
$ cd bin
```

```session
$ pwd
/usr/bin
```

Notice what we typed: `bin`, not `/usr/bin`. There is no `/` at the start. That
makes it a **relative path** - it is read starting from where you are, not from
the root.

The rule is short, and it is worth memorising:

* A path starting with `/` is **absolute**. It starts at the root.
* A path not starting with `/` is **relative**. It starts at your present
  working directory.

So `cd bin` only works when you happen to be in `/usr`. Try it from your home
directory and you will get `No such file or directory`, because there is no
`bin` inside `/home/anand`. The same words mean different things depending on
where you are standing.

## Making a directory

The `mkdir` command makes a new directory.

Let's go home and make one:

```session
$ cd
```

```session
$ mkdir notes
```

Like `cd` and `touch`, it prints nothing when it works. Let's look:

```session
$ ls
hello.txt  notes  notes.txt  numbers.txt  todo.txt
```

There is `notes`, alongside the files we made in the previous chapter. (Yes,
there is both a `notes` directory and a `notes.txt` file. They are different
things with similar names, and the computer has no trouble telling them apart.)

If you try to make it again, `mkdir` refuses:

```session
$ mkdir notes
mkdir: cannot create directory ‘notes’: File exists
```

That is a useful refusal. If `mkdir` had quietly succeeded, it might have
thrown away whatever was in there.

Now let's go into it:

```session
$ cd notes
```

```session
$ pwd
/home/anand/notes
```

```session
$ ls
```

Nothing. A brand new directory is empty.

## Building a small tree

We are inside `notes`. Let's make a directory for each week of the course.

```session
$ mkdir week1
```

```session
$ ls
week1
```

```session
$ mkdir week2
```

```session
$ mkdir week3
```

```session
$ ls
week1  week2  week3
```

We have built this:

```
/home/anand
└── notes
    ├── week1
    ├── week2
    └── week3
```

## Putting files in them

Let's go into `week1` and write down what we covered.

```session
$ cd week1
```

```session
$ pwd
/home/anand/notes/week1
```

```session
$ echo the command line > topics.txt
```

```session
$ ls
topics.txt
```

```session
$ cat topics.txt
the command line
```

Nothing new here - this is `echo`, `>` and `cat` from the previous chapter. What
is new is *where* the file went. `topics.txt` was created in the directory we
were standing in, which was `week1`. Commands act on the present working
directory unless you tell them otherwise.

## Going up

We are in `week1`. How do we get back to `notes`?

Every directory contains a special name, `..`, which means "the directory above
this one".

```session
$ cd ..
```

```session
$ pwd
/home/anand/notes
```

`..` is a relative path like any other, so it can be part of a longer one. From
`notes`, we can go into `week2` and create a file there:

```session
$ cd week2
```

```session
$ echo files and directories > topics.txt
```

Now, still standing in `week2`, we can read the file in `week1` without moving:

```session
$ cat ../week1/topics.txt
the command line
```

Read that path from left to right: go up one level (to `notes`), then into
`week1`, then take `topics.txt`. We never left `week2` - `pwd` will confirm it.

You can use `..` more than once. From `week2`, going up twice lands you in your
home directory:

```session
$ cd ../..
```

```session
$ pwd
/home/anand
```

Let's fill in `week3` too, using a relative path instead of walking there:

```session
$ echo pipes and filters > notes/week3/topics.txt
```

```session
$ cat notes/week3/topics.txt
pipes and filters
```

We are still in `/home/anand`. The path `notes/week3/topics.txt` was read
starting from here.

::: {.callout-tip}
There is also `.`, a single dot, which means "this directory". So
`./topics.txt` and `topics.txt` mean exactly the same thing. It looks pointless
now, but it becomes useful later.
:::

## The same file, three ways

We are in our home directory. Here is `week1`'s file, reached by a relative
path:

```session
$ cat notes/week1/topics.txt
the command line
```

And here is the very same file, reached by an absolute path:

```session
$ cat /home/anand/notes/week1/topics.txt
the command line
```

And once more, from inside `week2`:

```session
$ cd notes/week2
```

```session
$ cat ../week1/topics.txt
the command line
```

One file, three ways of naming it. The absolute path is the longest, but it is
the only one that works from anywhere - the other two depend on where you are
standing. That is the whole difference between the two kinds of path.

## A shortcut for home

Your home directory comes up constantly, so the shell gives it a short name:
`~`, the tilde character.

```session
$ cd ~
```

```session
$ pwd
/home/anand
```

`~` expands to the full path of your home directory, so `~/notes/week1` and
`/home/anand/notes/week1` are the same place. Because it starts from a fixed
point rather than from where you are, it behaves like an absolute path:

```session
$ cd /usr/bin
```

```session
$ cat ~/notes/week1/topics.txt
the command line
```

This is also what the `~` in your prompt means. When the prompt reads
`anand@laptop:~$`, it is telling you that you are in your home directory.

## Summary

| Command | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `pwd` | prints where you are |
| `cd /usr/bin` | goes to `/usr/bin`, from anywhere |
| `cd bin` | goes into `bin`, inside where you already are |
| `cd` | goes back to your home directory |
| `cd ..` | goes up one level |
| `cd ../..` | goes up two levels |
| `cd ~` | goes to your home directory |
| `mkdir notes` | makes a directory named `notes` |
| `cat notes/week1/topics.txt` | reads a file in another directory |

And the one idea to carry forward: a path starting with `/` is read from the
root, and a path that does not is read from wherever you are standing.
